text:
Toronto Registry No. D170/85

DATE:   1988·II·29

CITATION:
Lusher v. Lusher

THE  ONTARIO  PROVINCIAL
COURT

(FAMILY  DIVISION)

IN THE MATTER OF an application
for access to Brandon Lusher (an Infant) pursuant to the provisions of the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1980, c. 68, as amended by S.O. 1982, c. 20;

BETWEEN:

SYLVIA  LUSHER,

Applicant,

—  AND  —

HARRIS  LUSHER  and  NANCY
LUSHER,

Respondents.

Before Provincial Judge David R. Main

Heard on 18-21
January 1988; and 1 February 1988

Reasons for
Judgment released on 29 February 1988

ACCESS TO CHILD — General — Rights of
non-parent — Grandparent — Whether access would prove to be positive experience
for child — Paternal grandmother applied for access to child (now 4½ years old)
over opposition of father and child’s mother — Father’s own childhood and
adolescence had been so excessively controlled by grandmother that, once he
broke free of her, he wanted as little to do with her as possible — His
marriage was not to her liking and both he and his wife feared that grandmother
would exploit access (regardless of what form it would take) as vehicle to
undermine their marriage and to reassert her control over him — To avoid her
interference in their lives, father and wife refused her any access — Attempts
at mediation between parties collapsed when even experienced professionals
could not control grandmother’s ranting, raving and outpouring of verbal venom
— Court pointed out that access was right of child and not that of grandparent
or any other person and that court would grant it only if it served child’s
best interests — In this case, grandmother’s ambition to suppress father’s
independence from her would manifest itself in during any access to grandson by
her derogatory remarks about his parents’ marriage and about his mother —
Grandmother simply had no appreciation of what was in boy’s best interests and
of how her remarks would affect him — Access should not be allowed in hostile
environment that could undermine or endanger child’s stability or would
otherwise pose risk to child’s safety and comfort — Access by this grandmother
would be negative experience that would not serve child’s best interests —
Access denied.

STATUTES AND REGULATIONS CITED

Children’s Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1980, c. 68 [as amended by S.O. 1982, c. 20], section 21,
subsection 24(1), subsection 24(2) and clause 24(2)(
g
).

Office of the Official Guardian, legal representative for the child

[
1
]

PROVINCIAL JUDGE D.R. MAIN:—  The
applicant, Sylvia Lusher, seeks an order for access to her 4½-year-old
grandson, Brandon.  Her application is opposed by Brandon’s parents, Harris and
Nancy Lusher, and by counsel on behalf of the Official Guardian.  From the time
of his birth, the applicant has only seen Brandon on approximately six occasions,
the last visit taking place some 2½ years ago.

[
2
]

The application, which was commenced almost
three years ago, is unique in many respects, but primarily because of the
intransigence and the overwhelming hostility demonstrated by the litigants.
Intervention by mental health professionals at the Family Court Clinic, the
office of the Official Guardian and the Jewish Family and Child Service of Metropolitan
Toronto resulted in identification of the emotional issues in conflict but has
failed to resolve or even begin to resolve them.

[
3
]

The applicant is a hard-working and very
determined individual.  Unfortunately, her personality is such that she is
obsessed with an unhealthy desire to continue to control her son as she did
when he was a child, even though he is now 34 years of age, married and a
parent.  The applicant is convinced, albeit wrongly, that her daughter-in-law,
with the use of her body, has been able to capture her son’s mind and she has
desperately sought and continues to seek an opportunity to lure her son back to
her and to undo the entanglement.  Were she given the opportunity, the result
would most assuredly mean an end to the respondents’ marriage.  It is this
disaster that the respondents fear and one that they believe would flow from
supervised or unsupervised access during which the applicant would, they
believe, deliberately cast Brandon’s mother and their marriage in an
unfavourable light.

[
4
]

The applicant’s passion to manipulate and
retrieve her son has been so intense that she has often misconstrued or failed
to understand words and events pertaining to their relationship and has
typically over-reacted or reacted inappropriately.  Although vehemently opposed
to the request for access, the respondents have by and large withdrawn from
conflict initiated by the applicant.  In such circumstances, an accurate
historical recall by the applicant would be exceptionally difficult and,
accordingly, wherever the evidence is disparate, the version offered by the
respondents is to be preferred.

[
5
]

To more fully understand the nature of the
dispute and the complex human relationships and personalities upon which it is
based, it is necessary to review in some detail the relevant history of the
parties.

[
6
]

Harris Lusher was born in New York City and
was raised primarily by his mother and his maternal uncle, Abe Silver.  His
parents’ marriage lasted for a very short period of time and he really had no
opportunity to get to know or to have a meaningful parent-ans-child relationship
with his father, who had moved to Florida.  Access to his father was only
periodic and often traumatic because of the emotional stress placed upon such
meetings by his mother.  Harris recollects being used as a tool to extract
support money from his father and of being told that his father was “a bum” and
a deserter and that he and his parents were “communists” and had threatened to
kidnap him and take him away to Russia.  In light of these statements made by
his primary caretakers, it is entirely understandable that any young child
would be apprehensive at the prospect of access visits.  In Harris’ case, the
apprehension manifested itself through fear of his father, severe anxiety and
even nausea.  His belief in the truth of these allegations was maintained until
early adolescence and only now is Harris beginning to understand his father and
to build a meaningful relationship with him.

[
7
]

Throughout the years, and particularly in
his childhood, the applicant has excessively intruded upon her son’s life.  As
a child, Harris was grossly overprotected and controlled and he was never
allowed, nor was he able to complete, a normal sibling separation process from
his mother.

[
8
]

While the family lived in New York, Harris
was never allowed to go out unaccompanied after school other than to the
synagogue.  Unlike his peers, he was prevented from attending camp, from riding
into Manhattan on the subway, from going ice skating or to the movies and from
playing baseball.  On one occasion when he happened to stay at a synagogue
dance after 11:00 p.m., his uncle and mother waited outside to escort him four
blocks to the family home.  He was denied the opportunity to spend a religious
weekend at the home of a rabbi.  Ignoring medical advice, the applicant
encouraged Harris to continue to eat excessively, resulting in a body weight of
177 pounds by the time the boy reached Grade V.  He was allowed to have friends
over to his home after school hours, but only because his activities and
whereabouts could be monitored and controlled.

[
9
]

Harris’ efforts to reason with his
domineering mother inevitably led to arguments and then simply ended with the
issues remaining unresolved.  He chose to live with the situation rather than
endure further confrontation and this stance continued until he finally moved
out of the home just prior to his marriage.  Harris has never come to grips
with the reality of his relationship with his mother which is a fundamental
issue in the proceeding.  Thus, he must shoulder some of the responsibility for
this contest over access.

[
10
]

To her credit, the applicant has always
encouraged Harris to excel in his studies and he ultimately graduated from the
University of Toronto with a bachelor’s and a master’s degree in science.  In
addition, the applicant and Mr. Silver encouraged Harris to pursue a musical
hobby, which, in his adult years, led to the acquisition of sufficient skill to
enable him to perform with bands.  The path to that end was not without incident,
hoerver, as Harris was not allowed, as an adolescent, to choose a guitar
amplifier that he wanted and, when he disobeyed his mother and took the
amplifier chosen for him out of the home to practise, his guitar strings were
taken away.

[
11
]

To some extent, one can understand and
appreciate the concern that the applicant had for her son’s safety and
wellbeing in the city of New York during the 1960s.  On balance, however, her
concern and the restrictions that she placed upon her son as he matured were
far too excessive and robbed him of the opportunity to experience many normal
childhood activities and to explore and absorb the world around him.

[
12
]

Two significant events prompted the
applicant and Mr. Silver to leave New York City with Harris, who was 17 at the
time, and to move to Toronto.  When Harris was 15 years of age, he was
seriously assaulted by another youth outside of his school.  When the applicant
failed to convince the police to charge the other youth and rather than dealing
with it through the school, she simply withdrew her son from school for a
substantial period of time.  Subsequently, during the course of a robbery at
their business, Mr. Silver was shot and the applicant assaulted.

[
13
]

Once settled in Toronto, the applicant and
Mr. Silver carried on in retail business and Harris completed his education.
To the detriment of everyone, the applicant continued to interfere with and
manipulate Harris and he continued to accept the situation.  When Harris was 21
years old, the applicant managed to break up his first serious relationship
with a girl who tearfully counselled him “to run”.  He neither ran nor did
anything to alter the
status quo
at home.

[
14
]

In the fall of 1976, when he was studying
for his undergraduate degree, Harris met and began dating Nancy, the girl who
would ultimately become his wife.  Their relationship grew and, in February
1978, they became engaged and were married four months later.  In September
1983, Brandon was born.  From his birth to the commencement of this application
in March 1985, the applicant had only limited access to her grandson and a
denial of further access resulted in the applicant’s seeking relief through the
court process.

[
15
]

To begin with, the relationship between the
applicant and Nancy was cool and civil.  Over time, it deteriorated into a
bitter feud that, on one occasion, resulted in the applicant’s physically
assaulting Harris, purportedly as a result of his conduct in attending at a
baseball game rather than cutting the hedge, and verbally assailing Nancy’s
moral character.  Although Nancy attempted rapprochement with the applicant, in
the end she withdrew from contact in order to protect herself from a situation
that she rightly believed would never succeed and could only damage her
marriage to Harris.  The applicant presumed that Nancy had something in her
background to hide and she probed for facts to substantiate her belief.  Ultimately,
the applicant concluded that Harris’ marriage to Nancy would fail and she
openly proclaimed her view.  In these circumstances, it is not surprising that
the applicant was not asked to participate in the planning of the wedding as is
traditional.  What is surprising is that the applicant learned of the
engagement from a third party and not from her son.  The fact of the engagement
did not diminish the applicant’s desire to prevent the wedding.  In the presence
of Harris, Nancy and Nancy’s parents, the applicant loudly and vigorously
announced that the wedding would not take place.  A few days before the event,
she telephoned the rabbi who was to officiate at the ceremony and requested
that he decline to do so.  The wedding took place as scheduled and, although
the applicant attended, her sadness and displeasure were visibly evident.

[
16
]

With the birth of Brandon, the distance
between the antagonists widened.  From practically the moment of Brandon’s
birth, the applicant took the position that her daughter-in-law’s intentions
were to restrict and make access difficult.  She was wrong.  Any conditions set
by Nancy were reasonable, given the employment, health and housing stresses being
experienced by her and Harris and her concern for adequate hygiene and sickness
prevention as it relates to a newborn.  It is difficult to understand the hurt
that the applicant expressed at not being offered her grandson to hold at his
circumcision ceremony when she, on at least two occasions in the presence of
Harris, seriously questioned the child’s paternity.

[
17
]

The “final straw” for Harris and Nancy came
when, without any reasonable foundation in fact, the applicant reported to the
Jewish Family and Child Service of Metropolitan Toronto that Brandon might be
suffering from seizures and that his parents were neglecting his health.  The
allegations stemmed from an incident when Brandon was approximately three months
old.  The child had been left in the care of his grandmother while his parents
attended a movie.  He began to cry and squirm and it took 1½ hours for the
applicant to quiet him.  The applicant diagnosed the situation as some form of
epilepsy and, when Harris and Nancy failed to react to the alarm that she felt,
she took the very serious step of involving a children’s aid society.  The
resulting investigation concluded nothing untoward in regard to the child’s
status.  In fact, Brandon has always been a fundamentally healthy child and his
parents have always properly addressed his medical and emotional needs in all respects.

[
18
]

Once the access issue was before the court,
the matter was referred to the Family Court Clinic for assessment.  After a
comprehensive investigation, the clinic recommended,
inter alia
, that
there be no access at the present time and that the parties enter into some
form of mediation over a period of a year.  Subsequently, meetings were held
with social workers at the Jewish Family and Child Service of Metropolitan
Toronto.  That process produced no resolution of any of the outstanding issues.

[
19
]

During the course of the clinic assessment,
the applicant and Mr. Silver alleged that Nancy’s father had assaulted them in
a subway station.  He was charged and, after a full hearing, the charges were
dismissed.  The applicant was dissatisfied with the recommendations of the
clinic and the treatment she received from the staff at the Jewish Family and
Child Service of Metropolitan Toronto and she caused investigations to be
conducted at very high levels in the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of
Community and Social Services.  Both investigations found no improprieties.
Included in the applicant’s criticism of the assessment process at the clinic was
an allegation, totally without foundation, that the primary assessor had made
her recommendations after acceptance of a bribe from counsel on behalf of the
respondents.

[
20
]

The applicant and Mr. Silver have formed an
organization called “Heritage for Children” with which they hope to advance
access rights for grandparents.  They have been active in pursuing their goal
to the extent of mentioning their own situation during the course of media
interviews.  As with other gossip generated in the community by the applicant,
the attendant publicity has adversely affected Harris and Nancy.

[
21
]

Subsection 24(1) of the
Children’s Law
Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1980, c. 68, as added by S.O. 1982, c. 20, makes it perfectly
clear that the merits of an application for access to a child must be
determined on the basis of the best interests of the child.

[
22
]

The special relationship of a grandparent
and grandchild and a consideration of that relationship as it affects access is
acknowledged by clause 24(2)(
g
) of the Act, which directs the court,
when determining the best interest of a child, to consider “the relationship by
blood  . . .  between the child and each person who is a
party to the application”.

[
23
]

The right of a grandparent, or for that
matter any person, to apply for an order for access when it has been denied is
enshrined in s. 21 of the Act. The focus of such an application as it relates
to grandparent applicants has been succinctly stated by Provincial Judge F.
Stewart Fisher at page 9 of his judgment in
Wylde
v. Wylde
,
1984 CanLII 91
, 28 A.C.W.S. (2d) 404, [1984] W.D.F.L. 1671, 3
&
4 O.L.W.C.D. 229, [1984] O.J. No. 764
, 1984 Cars­well­Ont 1693 (Ont.
Prov. Ct., Fam. Div.):

[29]
It
is clear from the law under the
Children’s Law Reform Act
, as well as
the thrust of literature on the subject, that grandparent access is a right
of the child and not the grandparent.  Grandparents have a right to apply for
status and to be heard.  Historically, they have never had an absolute right
to access over the parents’ wishes.  The first and most important question to
be asked in these matters is: “Is it in the best interest of the child to
visit a grandparent?”  Will the child benefit from such access either
actually or potentially, or will the child be affected adversely, either
actually or potentially
?

[
24
]

Grandparent and extended family access to a
child is important, and particularly so as the traditional stable nuclear
family becomes less and less a societal norm.  Disintegration of a nuclear
family unit has the potential to interrupt or to hinder the development of meaningful
and positive extended family bonds to the detriment of the children involved.
Where access with a grandparent will be a positive experience for a child, the
court will ensure that such access is maintained:
Vormittag
and Vormittag v. Vormittag
,
1984 CanLII 90
, 29 A.C.W.S. (2d) 114, [1985]
W.D.F.L. 338, [1984] O.J. No. 760, 1984 Cars­well­Ont 1700 (Ont. Prov. Ct.,
Fam. Div.).  Where such access will be exercised in some form of hostile environment
that cannot be alleviated and that could undermine or endanger the stability of
the child or would otherwise present a risk to the child’s safety and comfort,
contact should be denied:
Greber
v. Moskowitz
,
1982 CanLII 74
, [1982] W.D.F.L. 1249, [1982] O.J. No.
595, 1982 Cars­well­Ont 1844 (Ont. Prov. Ct., Fam. Div.);
Tramble
v. Hill
,
1987 CanLII 1201
, 7 R.F.L. (3d) 85, [1987] O.J. No. 1450, 1987
Cars­well­Ont 307 (Ont. U.F.C.);
Milne v. Milne
(1985),
1985 CanLII 786 (BC CA)
, 44 R.F.L. (2d)
241, [1985] B.C.J. No. 1853, 1985 Cars­well­BC 508 (B.C.C.A.);
Wylde
v. Wylde
,
supra
.

[
25
]

The applicant seeks access to her grandson,
supervised or unsupervised, and on any terms and conditions imposed by the
court.  The respondents believe that it would not be in the best interests of
their son to have access to his grandmother at this point in time.  They are
prepared to reconsider the issue at Brandon’s request once he turns 13 years of
age, has had his Bar Mitzvah and, as a young adult, is capable of better coping
with any stresses which might result.

[
26
]

The overwhelming conclusion that must be
reached in this case is that, at this point in time, it would not be in the
best interests of Brandon for the applicant to have access to him.
Accordingly, the application will be dismissed.

[
27
]

The fundamental weaknesses in the applicant’s
position are her intense desire to regain control of her son, thereby
emasculating any semblance of independence that he may have achieved, and the
certainty that she will use any avenue open to her to achieve that end.  The
risk is just too great that, in the presence of Brandon, the applicant will make
derogatory remarks with respect to Harris’ marriage and Brandon’s mother, which
could have the effect of emotionally scarring Brandon and of weakening or
destroying his parents’ marriage.  The outcome of two meetings at the Jewish
Family and Child Service of Metropolitan Toronto demonstrates without qualification
that the applicant cannot control herself nor can she be controlled even by
experienced professionals.  During the course of those meetings and in the face
of the applicant’s ranting, raving and outpouring of verbal venom, the social
workers involved simply gave up in attempting to focus the applicant and Mr.
Silver on mediation.  There is no condition of supervision that the court could
impose that would obstruct the applicant from the path that she has chosen.  In
any event, supervised access should only normally be ordered as an interim
measure when moving toward unsupervised access.  The desirability of that end
has not been demonstrated.

[
28
]

The applicant may love her grandson, but she
has no appreciation of what is in his best interests and of what the impact
upon him would be should he hear his mother bitterly criticized or should his
nuclear family disintegrate.  It is an absolute certainty that, if there were
an access order, the applicant would at some point in time exceed the bounds of
acceptable familial discourse.  Once spoken, words designed to hurt could never
to retracted or forgotten.  The impact upon Brandon would be devastating.

[
29
]

It is important for Brandon to know and
appreciate his roots and his culture.  In large measure, that is being
accomplished by the regular and ongoing contact that he has with both of his
grandfathers.  It is unfortunate that he will not have a chance to develop a
relationship at this time with his paternal grandmother, particularly since his
maternal grandmother is deceased.  However, on balance, his emotional health
and the stability of his nuclear family are much more important considerations.
Brandon knows he has a paternal grandmother and has seen photographs of her.
Should he question her absence from his life, his parents must respond in a
sensitive and fair fashion regardless of the animosity they harbour toward the
applicant.  They would do their son a disservice if they did otherwise.

[
30
]

In his submissions, counsel on behalf of the
respondents sought orders restraining the applicant from contacting his clients
and from embarrassing them in the public media. Such relief was not formally
sought in the respondent’s pleadings, and cannot be claimed at the conclusion
of the trial.

[
31
]

Taking into consideration the result and the
conduct of the applicant prior to and during the litigation, this is an
appropriate case for costs:
Andrews v. Andrews
(1980),
1980 CanLII 1913 (ON CA)
, 32 O.R. (2d) 29,
120 D.L.R. (3d) 252, 20 R.F.L. (2d) 348, 20 C.P.C. 88, [1980] O.J. No. 3887,
1980 Cars­well­Ont 323 (Ont. C.A.).  Counsel are at liberty to arrange an
assessment hearing before me to address the basis upon which the award should
be made and the quantum.
